Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

vignette:
Liam is a 25-year-old salesperson who lives with his girlfriend, Maya, in a mid-sized American city. He came to therapy at Maya's urging, though he admits he has been struggling for nearly two years. Before that, he had just finished a brief contract working for a non-governmental organization in a conflict zone overseas-a job he took right out of college, believing he could make a difference. He had never expected to become a civilian in an active war zone.

The event that changed everything happened on a Tuesday afternoon. Liam was riding in a convoy of aid vehicles through a market district when the street erupted. He remembers the sound first-a crack so loud it seemed to split the air itself-and then the screaming. A mortar had struck a stall fifty yards ahead. He saw bodies on the ground, people running, a child being carried by a man whose face was covered in blood. His driver reversed hard, and Liam was thrown against the door. For what felt like hours, they sat pinned in traffic while small arms fire popped in the distance. He remembers the smell of diesel and dust, and the wet, metallic scent of blood that seemed to cling to the inside of the vehicle even after they finally escaped. No one in his convoy was killed, but Liam saw everything.

In the weeks that followed, he finished his contract and returned home. At first, he told himself he was fine. He went back to work at a car dealership, stood on the lot in his pressed shirt, and smiled at customers. But something was wrong. He found it impossible to concentrate. A customer would be telling him about their budget, and Liam's mind would drift to the texture of the dust on his hands that day. He would miss key details, forget to mention financing options, and lose sales. His manager pulled him aside twice to ask if he was okay. Liam said he was tired.

The nights were the worst. He had come to believe that darkness itself was dangerous. When the sun went down, a low, grinding fear settled in his chest. He would check the locks on the apartment door three or four times before bed. He insisted on keeping a lamp on in the hallway. If Maya got up to use the bathroom, the sound of her footsteps in the dark would make his heart hammer so hard he felt dizzy. He was certain that something terrible could happen at any moment, that safety was an illusion that evaporated with the daylight. He had never felt this way before, and he could not explain it to her without sounding insane.

What frightened Liam most was not the memory itself, but the way it came with a feeling he could not control. When he thought about that afternoon, his stomach would drop, his palms would sweat, and a wave of horror would wash over him as if it were happening again. He felt guilty for being alive, for having left, for not helping the child he saw. He felt ashamed that he could not simply get over it. He began to avoid anything that reminded him of that place: news reports about conflict, movies with explosions, even the smell of diesel at a gas station. He started taking a longer route to work to avoid a construction site where a jackhammer sounded too much like gunfire.

The consequences accumulated. He stopped going out with friends. He canceled dinner plans because he felt too on edge. Maya grew frustrated, then worried. She told him he was not the same person. He knew she was right. He had become a man who lived in a state of constant low-grade dread, who could not concentrate on a sales pitch, who lay awake at night listening for sounds that were not there. When his PCL-5 score came back at 76, the clinician explained that this was severe. Liam just nodded. He already knew.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a moment three weeks ago. He was standing on the dealership lot at dusk, and a car backfired in the street. He dropped to the ground behind a sedan, his hands over his head, his breath coming in ragged gasps. A customer saw him. His manager saw him. He was sent home. That night, Maya sat him down and said, quietly, that she could not watch him fall apart anymore. Liam agreed to come here, but he is not sure what he hopes for. He is afraid that talking about it will make it worse. He is afraid that the fear will never leave. But he is also afraid of losing Maya, and of losing himself entirely to a day that already took everything it could.
